paragraphs: Nothing, it would seem, could be better suited to arouse and feed curiosity than the sight of the United States. Fortunes, opinions, and laws there are in ceaseless variation; it is as if unchanging nature herself had become changeable, so great are the alterations the hand of man works upon her. Yet in the end the sight of this excited community becomes monotonous, and after watching the moving pageant for a time, the spectator grows tired of it. Among aristocratic nations every man stays pretty much in his own sphere, but men are astonishingly unlike one another — their passions, ideas, habits, and tastes are essentially different. Nothing changes, but everything differs. In democracies, on the contrary, all men are alike and do much the same things. It is true that they are subject to great and frequent reversals; but because the same events of good or bad fortune keep recurring, only the names of the actors change, and the play is always the same. The aspect of American society is lively, because men and things are always changing; but it is monotonous, because all these changes are alike.

Men living in democratic ages have many passions, but most of their passions either end in the love of riches or come from it. The reason is not that their souls are narrower but that money truly matters more in such times. When all the members of a community are independent of one another or indifferent to one another, the cooperation of each can be obtained only by paying for it. This multiplies endlessly the uses to which wealth can be put, and raises its value. When the reverence that once belonged to what is old has vanished, birth, condition, and profession no longer distinguish men, or hardly do so at all. Almost nothing but money remains to create strongly marked differences among them and to lift some above the common level. The distinction that springs from wealth grows as every other distinction disappears or shrinks. Among aristocratic nations money reaches only a few points on the vast circle of human desires; in democracies it seems to lead to all of them. The love of wealth can therefore be traced, as a chief or a secondary motive, at the bottom of everything the Americans do. This gives all their passions a kind of family likeness and soon makes the survey of them exceedingly wearisome. This perpetual recurrence of the same passion is monotonous; the particular means by which the passion seeks its own satisfaction are no less so.

In an orderly and settled democracy like the United States, where men cannot get rich by war, by public office, or by political confiscation, the love of wealth drives them chiefly into business and manufacturing. Although these pursuits often cause great upheavals and disasters, they cannot prosper without strictly regular habits and a long routine of small, uniform acts. The stronger the passion, the more regular these habits and the more uniform these acts. It may be said that the violence of their desires is what makes the Americans so methodical; it disturbs their minds, but it disciplines their lives.

The remark I apply here to America could in fact be made of almost all our contemporaries. Variety is disappearing from the human race; the same ways of acting, thinking, and feeling are found all over the world. This is not only because nations have more influence on one another and imitate one another more faithfully. It is also because the men of each country give up more and more the distinctive opinions and feelings of a caste, a profession, or a family, and so arrive together at something nearer to the nature of man, which is the same everywhere. Thus they grow more alike, even without having imitated one another. Picture travelers scattered through a large forest crossed by paths that all converge on one point. If every one of them keeps his eyes fixed on that point and moves toward it, they draw imperceptibly closer together, though they do not seek one another, do not see one another, and do not know one another; and they will be surprised in the end to find themselves all gathered on the same spot. All the nations that take as the object of their studies and their imitation not any particular man but man himself are tending in the end toward a similar state of society, like these travelers converging on the central clearing of the forest.
